<reason>B wins by distinguishing broad open licensing from guaranteed, usable research access and defending an enforceable alternative. Its direct pressure answers establish immediate reuse permissions, institutional responsibility, and scheduled releases, undermining A’s repeated claim that researchers must await an absent investigator’s generosity. A establishes a genuine friction advantage and a plausible default for routine outputs, but inadequately addresses community interests outside existing legal protections and the consequences of irreversible mistaken release. B more successfully narrows and resolves the actual comparison.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s preservation-versus-licensing distinction, followed by its concrete grant-contract answer on post-grant permissions, defeats A’s strongest irreversibility argument. A’s closing still characterizes the alternative as merely promised future access despite B explicitly guaranteeing immediately exercisable research-reuse rights.</best_rebuttal>
